name: Verifying What a Model Produced
title: Verifying What a Model Produced
answer: Verifying what a model produced means checking an output against something other than the model itself: the source documents, a calculation, a rule, or a second system. It covers factual claims, citations, numbers, code, and the reasoning steps a model shows. In governance terms it is the control that sits between a generated draft and any decision, filing, or public statement made from it. The scope is narrower than model evaluation, which tests a system in general, and wider than proofreading, which checks only surface form.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Verifying what a model produced means checking an output against something other than the model itself: the source documents, a calculation, a rule, or a second system. It covers factual claims, citations, numbers, code, and the reasoning steps a model shows. In governance terms it is the control that sits between a generated draft and any decision, filing, or public statement made from it. The scope is narrower than model evaluation, which tests a system in general, and wider than proofreading, which checks only surface form.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Verification runs on the same retrieval and logging layers that feed the model, plus whatever holds the ground truth: source repositories, databases, tickers, filing archives, and version histories. A working setup keeps the prompt, the retrieved passages, the model version, and the raw output together so a reviewer can replay the run. Where outputs feed regulated work, the audit trail usually lives in the same system of record as the underlying transaction.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The common pattern is to decompose an output into checkable claims, then test each one against a named source. Numbers get recomputed, quotations get matched to the original, and citations get resolved to confirm the document exists and says what is claimed. Sampling is normal: reviewers check a fixed share of outputs at high stakes and a smaller share at low stakes, with thresholds set by the risk of the task. Where a claim cannot be traced, the usual practice is to mark it unresolved rather than accept or delete it silently.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Ownership matters more than tooling here. Someone has to be accountable for the check, and that person should not be the one who prompted the model. Records of what was verified, by whom, against which source, and on what date are what regulators and auditors ask for first.Provenance also runs the other way: a reader of the final document should be able to tell which parts came from a model and which did not.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect verification to move from a manual review step toward an instrumented one, with claim level metadata carried alongside the text. Standards work on content provenance and watermarking is still unsettled, so most organisations are building internal rules rather than waiting for a single external one. The harder problem is scale: review capacity grows linearly while generated volume does not. That gap is likely to push effort toward automated checking of the checks, and toward narrower use cases where the ground truth is already structured.
